paper.page: DAS et al.: RECALL-BOUNDED STALENESS FOR FILTERED MULTI-TENANT ANN GRAPH INDEXES 1 Recall-Bounded Staleness for Filtered Multi-Tenant ANN Graph Indexes under Concurrent Updates Namrata Das, Kailas Devadkar, Anand Godbole Sardar Patel Institute of Technology, Mumbai, India Abstract—Production vector search must continuously ingest, delete, and re-tenant vectors while serving low-latency, high- recall, metadata-filtered approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) queries for many tenants with per-tenant service-level objec- tives. Existing graph-based ANN systems address these require- ments largely in isolation, leaving recall during concurrent re- optimization without an analytical bound. We develop a graph- based index that combines streaming updates, filtered search, and multi-tenancy, with one theoretical result and two system mechanisms. Our theory decomposes per-tenant recall loss into staleness from updates not yet integrated into the graph and filtered navigability determined by the local density of points satisfying a tenant’s predicate. The staleness component exhibits anti-amortization on a merge-based graph, integrating a larger batch of inserts increases recall degradation super-linearly, so larger merges do not reduce total staleness loss. Holding the insert horizon fixed while increasing merge size 20×, we observe a monotonic decrease in terminal recall@10 from 99.44% to 99.01%. For filtered search, the theory gives a parameter-free frontier-mass relationship in local predicate density and a query- averaged per-tenant recall bound. We instantiate the bound with a filter and tenant-aware staging cache and a select-not-resize scheduler with per-tenant staleness ceilings. On a FreshDiskANN substrate, the ceiling eliminates tight-tier SLA violations under the evaluated churn workload, while merge reordering changes terminal recall by only 0.02 percentage points. The results show how recall bounds can guide background maintenance without relying on merge resizing as a recall control mechanism. Index Terms—Approximate nearest neighbor search, vector databases, graph indexes, streaming indexes, filtered search, multi-tenancy, recall, service-level objectives, index maintenance, concurrent updates. I. INTRODUCTION A WIDELY-HELD intuition about maintaining a graph- based approximate-nearest-neighbor (ANN) index under a stream of inserts is that batching amortizes cost, since folding more pending points into each merge lowers per-point maintenance overhead. This holds for throughput; for recall it does not. Integrating a batch of c inserts into a merge-based graph index degrades disk-graph recall@k super-linearly in c, so the total recall loss accumulated over an insertion horizon does not fall with the merge size. Larger, less frequent merges are no better for recall than smaller, more frequent ones, and on our point estimates they are worse. We call this anti- amortization. In practice only the weak form matters, since re-sizing merges cannot engineer degradation away and can only re-prioritize it, and this motivates the system we build. The design rests on the direction of the effect (L ∗ non- decreasing in c), which we measure on two independent axes; the magnitude of the super-linearity is less tightly pinned, and its per-merge-to-horizon assembly is a conservative step we find loose by about 2× (§V-B). Anti-amortization matters because the workloads that most need graph ANN are exactly the ones that mutate continuously. Production vector search must ingest, delete, and re-tenant vectors while serving low-latency, high-recall queries that carry metadata predicates, for many tenants each with its own service-level objective (SLO). Recent work names the pain directly. CANDOR-Bench [1] observes that under concurrency “throughput in concurrent settings is often constrained by in- sertion overhead rather than query latency, which highlights a mismatch between streaming workloads and designs originally tuned for offline construction.” The VDBMS Survey [2] places incremental k-NN among its open problems: e-commerce and recommender platforms retrieve an effectively very large k in small increments so that results appear seamlessly, and while techniques exist for that access pattern, “it is unclear how to support this search inside vector indexes.” A VLDB tutorial on filtered vector search [3] makes the corresponding point on the predicate axis, giving as a key objective “the importance of achieving stable recall, ideally in a declarative manner, ensuring consistent recall across queries.” And, from indus- try, Pinecone [4] reports that “data is continuously inserted and deleted, and metadata may be updated independently of the vector index, yet filters must be applied accurately and efficiently at query time.” The literature is heavily worked along each axis sep- arately but not at their intersection. Filtered-static graph ANN (Filtered-DiskANN, ACORN, RNSG, iRangeGraph, STABLE) builds one index over the joint feature-and- attribute space and does not stream. Streaming graph ANN (FreshDiskANN, SPFresh, Mycelium-Index, and the recent single-tenant SOTA PipeANN/OdinANN) operates on unfil- tered, single-tenant data and provides at best empirical recall stability under churn. Multi-tenant vector search (Curator, Pinecone, GaussDB-Vector) is sparse; Curator is static and in- memory, Pinecone sits on an IVF substrate with no analytical bound, and none schedules background work by per-tenant SLA. No prior system occupies their intersection, and none bounds the recall a tenant loses during live re-optimization of a filtered graph index. Our contribution occupies the axes those systems leave open, combining streaming, filtered, and multi-tenant oper- ation with per-tenant SLA scheduling, an analytical bound, and disk-resident scale. On the axes they do target, PipeANN and OdinANN lead single-tenant streaming and Curator leads static per-tenant recall, and we position against rather than arXiv:2610.15130v1 [cs.DB] 10 Oct 2026

DAS et al.: RECALL-BOUNDED STALENESS FOR FILTERED MULTI-TENANT ANN GRAPH INDEXES 2 displace them. We make one theoretical and two engineering contribu- tions. Our theorem (C1, §III) establishes the anti-amortization bound and generalizes it to the filtered, multi-tenant, deletes/migration setting. Its filtered term is a parameter- free frontier-mass law in the local predicate density σ loc that predicts the recovery scale L 95 = 1.25 k/σ loc and yields a per-tenant admission test 1.25 k/σ loc ≤ L max (ℓ τ ); evaluated as a query average, it is a conservative per-tenant recall lower bound. The staleness half is measured at horizon scale rather than extrapolated, with terminal recall decreasing monotoni- cally as the merge size grows across a 20× range of c. Two engineering designs instantiate the bound. A filter and tenant-aware staging cache (C2, §IV) absorbs in-flight inserts, deletes, and tenancy changes on the query path and collapses to the baseline on a single partition. An SLA- aware, select-not-resize scheduler (C3) honors a per-tenant max-staleness ceiling, re-prioritizing which pending work each fixed-size merge drains rather than re-sizing the merge that anti-amortization forbids. On a FreshDiskANN substrate we measure that anti- amortization holds end to end (at a fixed 60K-insert horizon, terminal recall@10 falls 99.44 → 99.01 as merges grow 1K → 20K), that re-ordering merges leaves terminal recall unchanged (|∆recall@10| = 0.02 pp), that the per-tenant staleness ceiling eliminates tight-tier SLA violations under churn where a ceiling-less baseline fails, and that the design remains memory-bounded and recall-correct at 100K. II. SYSTEM MODEL AND NOTATION Vectors, queries, predicates Let X ⊆ R d be the ambient space with metric ρ. A point x ∈ X carries metadata m(x) ∈ M; a predicate p : M → {0, 1} selects the filtered subset X p = {x : p(m(x)) = 1}, of global selectivity σ(p) = |X p |/|X |. A query is q = (v, k, p) with query vector v, neighbor count k, and predicate p; its ground truth is the k closest points of X p to v under ρ. Because filtered-graph recall is governed by predicate density near the query rather than globally (§III), we also define the query- joint local density σ loc (p, v) = Pr x∼nbhd(v) [p(m(x)) = 1], the fraction of v’s metric neighborhood that satisfies p. Tenants and SLOs The point set is marked by tenant: T is the tenant set and t(x) ∈ T each point’s tenant. A query has tenant scope T (q) ⊆ T (single-tenant when |T (q)| = 1); its effective candidate set is X p ∩{x : t(x) ∈ T (q)}. Each tenant τ carries a service-level objective SLO(τ ) = (ρ τ , ℓ τ ) (minimum recall ρ τ , maximum latency ℓ τ ) and a max-staleness ceiling S τ that the scheduler (§IV) honors. Graph index G = (V, E) is a directed graph over V ⊆ X built by Vamana (out-degree cap R, candidate width L, prune slack α > 1, pool cap maxc); Search(G, q, ef ) returns an approxi- mate top-k using exploration budget ef . The disk graph is a single label-blind Vamana: predicates and tenant labels are query-time post-filter tags and are never used in construction. This fact is central to both the theorem’s additivity and topology preservation (§III,§IV). Mutation streams Updates arrive as a marked point process M = {(s i , u i )} with u i ∈ {ins(x), del(x), mig(x, τ → τ ′ )} and per-class rates λ ins , λ del , λ mig . The toy setting (§III) is Poisson inserts-only (λ del = λ mig = 0); the general theorem admits all three (migration = a delete in τ plus an insert in τ ′ ). Cache, scheduler, compaction A filter-aware, tenant-aware staging cache C of capacity c holds pending mutations and is consulted on the query path, keyed by (p, T (q)). A priority-queue scheduler orders background graph-repair work by a composite key κ = α 1 stale + α 2 d ∆R + α 3 SLA + α 4 mig. Compaction fires a merge when cache occupancy reaches c (the theorem’s referent for c); the merge integrates the pending batch into G and resets the cache. Recall as a random variable For query q at time t, R q (t) = |(Search(G t , q, ef ) ∪ Cache t (q)) ∩ GT(q, t)|/k. The per-tenant recall is ¯ R τ (t) = E q [R q (t) | T (q) ∋ τ ], and the recall@k loss is L τ (t) = ρ τ − ¯ R τ (t). The object the theorem bounds is the worst-case over time of the query-averaged per-tenant loss on the horizon [0, T ], L ∗ τ = sup t∈[0,T ] L τ (t): worst-case in t, in expectation over q, so the guarantee is on the query average rather than on any individual query. III. THE RECALL-BOUNDED STALENESS THEOREM (C1) We first prove the central kernel in the toy setting (single tenant, no filter, inserts only), then lift it to the filtered, multi- tenant, deletes/migration setting. The staleness half of the bound is semi-empirical / loose-but-correct-form: its mech- anism and functional shape are derived and validated on two independent axes, while the exponents are calibrated. The filtered half is derived and parameter-free. We state this status precisely throughout. A. The toy bound: anti-amortization Definition 1 (Batch-merge operator M c ). Let G 0 be the disk graph over N points and B a batch of c pending inserts. M c (G 0 , B) acts in two phases. Forward: each x ∈ B obtains out-neighbors by greedy search against the frozen snapshot G 0 then ROBUSTPRUNE/α-RNG to degree R; G 0 is not mutated during the batch. Reconcile: each existing node unions its buffered reverse edges and re-prunes (on PQ distances) only if it exceeds R. Two structural consequences follow: (M1) the c batch points are mutually invisible during selection (no x ∈ B takes another batch point as a neighbor, unlike a from-scratch build); (M2) hubs flooded by batch reverse edges are re-pruned lossily on approximate distances.

The k-dependence of the law is a sharp untested prediction: h is a function of (βLσ loc , k) and not of x = σ loc L/k alone: at fixed x=1 it predicts 63.2/87.4/96.0% recall for k=1/10/100, whereas every measurement here is at k=10. The deletes floor g del 0 is parameterized but not yet characterized, and a first-principles derivation of the degra- dation exponents from α-RNG occlusion geometry is open; both remain open items. On the shared label-blind graph, filtered recall degrades with σ loc : the theorem’s content, not an unmodeled loss; a per-tenant-navigable structure removes it but cannot stream and carries no bound. In sum, three of Theorem 8’s four parts hold unconditionally (the additive assembly by subadditivity, the derived parameter- free filtered term, and the named measurable ANN deficit), while the staleness term is a calibrated scaling law (its pref- actor and exponents fit on one substrate, dataset family, and c/N range). The theorem is thus a proved decomposition of which one component is empirical: weaker than a distribution- free (ϵ, δ) guarantee, stronger than a recall estimator that predicts without constraining. A first-principles derivation of the degradation exponent would replace the calibration with a constant; we state it as open. IV. SYSTEM: CACHE (C2) AND SCHEDULER (C3) The two engineering contributions instantiate the theorem. C2 (the staging cache) absorbs within-cycle staleness on the query path so the loss the theorem bounds is the disk-graph term, not cache coverage; C3 (the scheduler) re-prioritizes background repair without ever re-sizing a merge, which is the only lever anti-amortization leaves. We prototype both on a FreshDiskANN fork with an io_uring backend. All numbers below are measured on this prototype unless marked otherwise. A. Substrate: one label-blind Vamana The disk index is a single Vamana graph over the label- agnostic vector set; predicates and tenant labels are query- time post-filter tags and never enter graph construction or the merge operator M c . Two properties follow, both central to §III. First, the per-merge degradation g(c, N ) is filter and tenant-independent (Assumption 5), the additivity hinge of Theorem 8. Second, a partition boundary can never induce topology degradation, because the graph never sees one; the scheduler’s re-ordering only changes which vectors co-merge and in what order. The prototype inherits the baseline’s merge exactly, and by design rather than by tuning: at every trigger all selected partitions are folded into one combined in-memory index and handed to one merge of size c, so the merge operator receives the same point set, at the same cadence, with the

DAS et al.: RECALL-BOUNDED STALENESS FOR FILTERED MULTI-TENANT ANN GRAPH INDEXES 6 same Merge Size as the unmodified baseline. Partitioning is therefore invisible to M c as a matter of code path, which is why the bound carries. We check that construction rather than infer it: with a single predicate and tenant the full C2+C3 pro- totype reproduces baseline post-merge recall@10 to δ=0.000 at three successive checkpoints (99.286/99.145/99.018, brute- force K=100 ground truth), with the ceiling-disabled, ceiling- never-firing, and FIFO legs byte-identical. B. C2: a filter-aware, tenant-aware staging cache FreshDiskANN stages pending inserts in two in-memory buffers double-buffered against the disk merge. We re-key each buffer to a hash map over partitions (predicate, tenant) and consult it on the query path, routing a query to its own partition and label-post-filtering disk results. The cache there- fore serves freshly-inserted, same-tenant points immediately, which is what makes filtering on the query path viable and is essential for filtered queries, since disabling the query-path keying costs 72–86 pp of per-label recall@10 at live cache occupancy (93.8/78.9/81.1 keyed vs. 7.8/7.3/7.6 unkeyed, at comparable p99, with identical probed staging occupancy in both legs so the staging state is held fixed). This ablation toggles more than a cache-probe comparison. A single query key drives both the cache probe and the disk post-filter, so the unkeyed leg is not a filter-blind cache alongside a correct disk path, since it pins every query’s key to one default partition, which simultaneously blinds the cache probe and points the disk post-filter at the wrong label for every tenant but one. The residual 7.5% is accordingly close to arithmetic, approximately the one correctly-keyed tenant’s share of the query mix times its recall. What the ablation establishes is that the query-path keying as a whole is central; it does not measure a cache-probe-only lift. Isolating the probe would require holding the disk post-filter on the true label while blinding only the cache, which the current knobs do not expose; the tighter comparator (a filter-blind cache that post-filters its own contents) is therefore not measured. The cache changes only what is staged and how queries route, not the merge cadence; at a merge, all selected partitions are folded into one combined in-memory index and drained as a single merge of size c (the combined-index single-merge drain), identical in topology to the baseline (merge-order parity δ=0.000). This is what lets the bound carry to the prototype unchanged. Unlike read-side or filter-blind caches over vector indexes (Ubis, MicroNN, QVCache), ours is jointly filter and tenant-keyed, on the query path, and is the exact structure the theorem binds. C. C3: an SLA-aware, select-not-resize scheduler The scheduler never re-sizes a merge; every fired merge is one combined fixed-size-c drain (bound-safe by construction, §IV-A), and it wins by selecting which pending work fills each merge and when. The rule follows from Theorem 3, by which re-sizing is not a recall lever in the first place, so there is nothing to gain, and from holding the merge at the baseline’s shape, which keeps the bound applicable without re- deriving it per configuration. An implementation observation that draining N partitions as N separate merges reads much worse (84.9/76.4/70.1) than the one-combined-merge design is not used as evidence, since it holds nothing fixed, and the design rule rests on the two reasons above. It orders background repair by a composite key κ(w, t) = α 1 stale(w, t)+α 2 d ∆R(w)+α 3 SLA(w)+α 4 mig(w), (9) over staleness, predicted recall impact, tightest tenant SLA, and migration cost, each min–max normalized across the pend- ing set at drain time. Exactly one of these terms is exercised in every measurement we report. The d ∆R term is implemented as an occupancy proxy behind a default-off flag and is disabled (α 2 =0) throughout, and no result depends on it. The migration term is identically zero in this prototype. The SLA term is inert whenever tenants share one SLO, since a term with a single distinct value normalizes to zero, and our churn legs additionally set α 3 =0 so that ceiling enforcement is the only variable. So κ reduces to staleness ordering (oldest-first) in all reported runs; deferred units reload as the oldest across the driver’s per-merge restart and drain first. The four-term form is the interface the scheduler exposes, not a mechanism this paper validates; the measured win below comes from the ceiling. On top of κ, a per-tenant max-staleness ceiling S τ force- drains a tenant whose staleness has reached S τ . This is a prioritization with a cadence-bounded overshoot, and the distinction matters for Theorem 8. The built scheduler tests ceilings only at a merge trigger, with no early-merge on crossing, so a tenant that crosses S τ mid-window stays stale until the next trigger. The guarantee we actually deliver is N stale τ ≤ λ (τ ) ins
S τ + W  , (10) where W is the trigger window (the high-water mark). The theorem’s λ (τ ) ins S τ cap is thus the W → 0 idealization; the prototype attains it up to one window, and we set W = S min τ to make that overshoot as small as the design admits without an early-merge mechanism. The effect is directly visible in our runs, where a tight tenant’s measured staleness reaches 1900 against a 1000 ceiling before the force-drain resets it, and in an earlier configuration (even with W set equal to S τ , the tightest the built cadence allows) the tight tier was still violated at one checkpoint on both legs for exactly this reason. Closing the gap would need an early-merge trigger. FIFO/threshold-triggered compaction (all prior streaming systems) has no per-tenant lever at all; §V-E shows the ceiling is what drives tight-tenant violations to zero under churn. D. Deletes and tenancy migration Deletes are tombstoned in the staging partitions and evicted at the combined merge; a tenancy migration is a delete in τ plus an insert in τ ′ . We extend the drain to evict tombstones from every partition (not only a default one), verified to conserve points (zero silently-dropped) and to leave deleted ids absent from post-merge results while survivors remain. This is what admits the deletes/migration term of Theorem 8; the term’s precise floor contribution g del 0 is not characterized here.

Recall–latency feasibility The admission test of Contribution C1 (1.25 k/σ loc ≤ L max (ℓ τ )) assumes search cost is linear in L; we measure it. Mean search latency is linear in L (mean(L) ≈ 0.22 ms · L + 1.6 ms, with mean disk IOs ≈ L exactly, since the search is IO-bound, one candidate ≈ one IO; Fig. 2), so the cost model holds and L max (ℓ τ ) ≈ ℓ τ /0.22 ms, giving the concrete feasibility condition σ loc ≥ 1.25 k / L max (ℓ τ ) ≈ 1.25 k · 0.22 ms/ℓ τ (e.g. ℓ τ = 50 ms ⇒ σ loc ≳ 0.055). (12) This prices the boundary of §V-F/§VII quantitatively: a σ loc = 0.01 tenant needs L 95 ≈ 1250, i.e. ≈ 275 ms mean, so it cannot hold a 95% recall floor and an interactive latency SLO on this substrate, and the test reports this before deployment (Fig. S2, supplementary material). We report the test on mean latency, with a ρ=0.95 floor and a candidate latency ladder (ℓ ∈ {10, 50, 200} ms). Since an interactive SLO is ultimately a tail guarantee, a low-contention p 99 capture would extend the test to the tail; the linear-cost and infeasibility conclusions here rest on the mean. E. Multi-tenant SLA under churn (the payoff axis) On an identical, genuinely-contended churn stream (T =6, tiers tight/medium/lax, ceilings 1000/3000/10 9 ), the C3 ceil- ing drives tight-tier SLA violations to zero at equal staleness and equal drained recall (82.34 vs. 82.22, i.e. enforcement costs nothing on terminal recall), where an otherwise-identical scheduler-less baseline violates every tight query (Table III). The medium tier is uneventful in this regime (zero violations on both legs), so the ceiling protects the tight tier only. Two qualifications bound the reading. The violation counted here is a per-tenant staleness-ceiling breach, staleness exceeding S τ , a freshness bound distinct from the recall/latency SLO (ρ τ , ℓ τ ). The baseline comparison is close to definitional (C3 force-drains at S τ ), so it establishes that the mechanism is implemented and effective; and the 100%-vs-0% split is a saturated margin (tight queries arrive in a burst inside the post-ceiling stale window), demonstrating the mechanism while the magnitude is specific to this 10K, three-checkpoint regime. The mechanism is not free in every regime; in an earlier configuration whose high-volume tier was the lax one, honoring tight ceilings deferred it and cost ≈10 pp of aggregate unfiltered recall at intermediate checkpoints (final topology unaffected by merge-order invariance). The substan- tive comparator is a per-tenant shard, against which ours is a rebuild-outage advantage: a shard is unqueryable for each cold rebuild, growing with per-tenant size (0.26 s at 1.8K/tenant to ≈ 28 s at 100K/tenant), while ours never rebuilds (no rebuild- induced serving outage; the index stays queryable through the background merge, which does inflate the tail for ≈ c/d s but

RNSG [7] and iRangeGraph [8] target range predicates; STA- BLE [9] fuses metric and attribute signals into one joint- semantic graph. All build a single static, single-tenant index over the joint space; we add streaming inserts/deletes/tenancy- migration, multi-tenant isolation, and an analytical bound. These designs secure same-label reachability at build time; our repair must preserve it under churn, which shapes the scheduler’s ordering. b) Streaming / dynamic graph ANN.: FreshDiskANN [10] (two-pass StreamingMerge, our substrate), SPFresh [11], IP-DiskANN [12], CleANN [13], Wolverine [14], and Mycelium-Index [15] operate on unfiltered, single-tenant data with at best empirical recall stability. PipeANN [16] (OSDI’25) and OdinANN [17] (FAST’26) are the current single-tenant SOTA, their pipelined-SSD search and direct-insert (no-merge) design sidestepping the scheduling problem we solve rather than solving it; neither has a tenant concept or a recall bound, so we cede the single-tenant axis and compare against a per-tenant sharding of each. LSM-VEC [18] organizes a vector index as an LSM tree, and UBIS [19] is the closest streaming competitor, scheduling concurrent updates to keep recall stable under high update rates but reporting that empirically with no bound. None provides filtering × multi-tenancy × a bound jointly. c) Multi-tenant ANN.: Curator [20] is the closest prior art, a multi-tenant graph ANN with per-tenant naviga- bility (clustering sub-trees) that is static and in-memory, with no per-tenant SLA scheduling and no bound; we build it and compare (conceding static recall, leading on streaming/SLA/bound/disk-scale). Pinecone Metadata Filter- ing [4] provides filter + multi-tenant + streaming on an IVF/serverless substrate with no analytical bound; GaussDB- Vector [21] is a production filtered vector database with real- time inserts/deletes but no per-tenant isolation, SLA schedul- ing, or bound. d) Caches over vector indexes.: MicroNN [22], QV- Cache [23], and LiveVectorLake [24] are read-side, or filter- /tenant-blind, or a different layer; our cache is jointly filter and tenant-keyed, on the query path, and is the structure the theorem binds. e) Theoretical bounds.: [25] bounds quantization un- der streaming updates, not a graph’s recall; Random-Walk Dynamic Graph ANN [26] bounds hitting-time topology preservation, not recall@k under an SLA; Quake [27] esti- mates recall for query-time parameters, not background work.
